# Overview: What “diurnal plankton periodicity” means in rivers

Diurnal periodicity refers to 24‑hour cycles in plankton abundance, biomass, and community composition that track environmental oscillations (day–night light, temperature, mixing) and biological processes (primary production, respiration, grazing, and vertical migrations). In rivers, these cycles operate within the reach-scale water column and are modulated by discharge, turbidity, and connectivity to lakes or floodplains. Across aquatic systems, diel rhythms are common and can encompass changes in population density, biomass, species composition, metabolic activity, and primary production, while also being influenced by sampling timing if measured at only a few day–night points. <cite id="75c05ea6-3">Diel patterns in phytoplankton are common and include cycles in population density, biomass, community composition, metabolism, resources, enzymatic activity, and primary production</cite> <cite id="75c05ea6-0">Earth’s rotation produces alternating light/dark diel cycles that entrain biological rhythms, with photoperiodic seasonal modulation</cite> <cite id="75c05ea6-3">Early field studies recognized these cycles and emphasized time-of-collection effects on observed plankton patterns</cite>.

# Evidence from rivers and reservoirs: diel rhythms are present

Field syntheses and case studies show clear diel rhythms in plankton that track abiotic cycles. In a tropical reservoir (Jos Plateau, Nigeria), diurnal fluctuations in temperature, dissolved oxygen, free CO2, alkalinity, and conductance were significant, and the study concluded that the diurnal cycle of environmental factors regulates diel movement (likely vertical positioning and activity) of plankters across seasons. <cite id="c7a4684e-1">Diurnal fluctuations in water temperature, dissolved oxygen, free carbon dioxide, total alkalinity and specific conductance were significant; this investigation describes the role of the diurnal cycle of various abiotic environmental factors in regulating the diurnal movement of plankters</cite>. In a Patagonian fjord influenced by river discharge, spectral analyses revealed a diurnal peak in backscatter (Sv) and instantaneous profiles exhibited banding dominated by diel variability; this diel vertical migration signal persisted even in austral autumn when zooplankton was least abundant, indicating ongoing nocturnal vertical movements. <cite id="c7a4684e-2">Semidiurnal peaks were associated with tides in the upper 10 m; spectra during autumn revealed a peak at the diurnal period, and diel vertical migrations were occurring as shown by instantaneous profiles and elevated backscatter bands dominated by diel variability</cite>. More broadly, diel oxygen dynamics in estuaries and rivers often reflect community metabolism, and high turbidity can damp diel amplitude by limiting phytoplankton production. <cite id="c7a4684e-0">Continuous measurements resolving diurnal variations in nutrients, turbidity, and chlorophyll would better explain diel-cycling dissolved oxygen; diel DO cycling was observed in the upper East River, but amplitudes were an order of magnitude smaller than in a nearby estuary, likely due to high turbidity limiting production</cite>.

At the scale of whole river basins, primary production curves measured over diel light–dark periods underpin integrated daily production. In the Congo River, daily integrated production in mainstem channels ranged from 64–434 mg C m−2 day−1 at falling water and 52–248 mg C m−2 day−1 at high water, with biomass restricted by hydrology but growth maintained by hydrologic processes; in the Danube, column production reached up to 12.6 g O2 m−2 day−1 in a lower-reach reach, illustrating strong spatial gradients. <cite id="47406f93-3">Daily integrated production in the Congo River varied between 64.3–434.1 mg C m−2 day−1 (falling water) and 51.5–247.6 mg C m−2 day−1 (high water), with hydrology maintaining biomass and enabling growth despite hydrological constraints</cite> <cite id="47406f93-3">Instantaneous fluorescence rise–relax ratio (FRRF) converted to daily integrals showed column production below 1 g O2 m−2 day−1 in the upper Danube and up to 12.6 g O2 m−2 day−1 at km 1262</cite>. These diel-driven production patterns provide the energetic basis for diurnal changes in phytoplankton abundance and zooplankton grazing pressure.

# Mechanisms: why diel cycles arise in river plankton

- Light-limited daytime production and night-time respiration/sinking. River phytoplankton typically increase production during daylight as light drives photosynthesis; at night, respiration and reduced buoyancy (higher densities) promote sinking and mixing losses, lowering surface biomass. In coastal systems, daytime microstratification can enhance in-situ production while nighttime cooling promotes convective mixing that redistributes biomass; similar hydrodynamic light coupling is widely invoked in rivers and lakes. <cite id="75c05ea6-2">Diel light:dark cycles regulate phytoplankton metabolism through photoperiod, night length, irradiance, and oscillation patterns</cite> <cite id="75c05ea6-3">Photosynthetic maxima in field phytoplankton were highest at noon with end-of-day variability; division patterns varied by species, indicating both environmental and endogenous controls</cite> <cite id="75c05ea6-4">Wavelet analyses show 24-hour periodicity in chlorophyll-related signals independent of tide; daytime thermal microstratification can cause net sedimentation while nighttime cooling drives net resuspension, altering vertical distributions</cite>.

- Zooplankton behavior and grazing. Zooplankton exhibit diel vertical migration (DVM), shifting into the photic zone at night to feed on daytime-produced phytoplankton and returning to depth during the day to avoid predation and high irradiance. Riverine DVM can be detected in backscatter and instantaneous vertical profiles, and discharge events can amplify or alter DVM intensity and vertical extent. <cite id="c7a4684e-2">Diel vertical migrations of zooplankton were indicated by increased backscatter around the pycnocline and throughout the water column, with timing and intensity influenced by riverine discharge pulses</cite> <cite id="47406f93-3">Zooplankton connects lower and higher trophic levels and is sensitive to environmental change; their community dynamics and interactions with phytoplankton shape planktonic structure</cite>. Export from adjacent lakes to receiving streams is accentuated during midday vertical migrations, routing daytime-grazed material downstream and reinforcing downstream diel signals. <cite id="47406f93-0">At a lake–stream interface, zooplankton were sampled over 24 h at 2–4 h intervals; midday vertical migration accentuates export of zooplankton from lakes to streams</cite>.

- Hydrologic forcing and turbidity. High suspended sediment and algal pigments reduce light penetration, compressing the photic zone and damping diel amplitude in both phytoplankton production and zooplankton visual navigation during DVM. Conversely, low-turbidity reaches and slack-flow periods allow stronger light-driven cycles. <cite id="c7a4684e-0">High turbidity in the upper East River limited primary production and reduced diel oxygen fluctuation amplitudes relative to clearer estuary sites</cite>.

- Seasonal and photoperiodic modulation. The length and intensity of day–night periods vary seasonally, which shifts phytoplankton physiology (e.g., diatom light:dark responses) and zooplankton foraging windows. Mixing events at night or during spring/autumn turnover modulate the strength of surface diel cycles. <cite id="75c05ea6-2">Photoperiod interacts with light intensity and oscillation pattern to modulate photosynthesis and metabolism in diatoms, with seasonal photoperiod changes at temperate latitudes</cite>.

# Magnitude, form, and context dependence

Diel amplitude depends on system size, turbidity, discharge, and season. In large lowland rivers and tropical systems, integrated daily production can range from tens to hundreds of mg C m−2 day−1, with daytime production dominating but biomass often constrained by hydrodynamics; floodplain connectivity can elevate production by adding lakes/reservoirs where phytoplankton accumulate for downstream export. <cite id="47406f93-3">Congo mainstem daily production was 64–434 mg C m−2 day−1 (falling water) and 52–248 mg C m−2 day−1 (high water), with hydrological processes maintaining biomass and enabling growth; connectivity to floodplains/natural lakes/reservoirs recruited phytoplankton to the main channel</cite> <cite id="47406f93-3">Danube column production peaked at 12.6 g O2 m−2 day−1 in a downstream reach</cite>. In a shallow river-fjord transition, diel backscatter variability dominated vertical profiles, indicating strong DVM-driven signals even when overall zooplankton abundance was low; discharge pulses introduced thermal and turbidity shifts that superimposed large diel-to-semidiel dynamics over a 13-hour peak in flow. <cite id="c7a4684e-2">Diel variability dominated instantaneous backscatter profiles, with discharge-peak timing (09:00) followed by elevated backscatter and temperature drop, and arrival of floodwaters by ~22:00 on the next day</cite>.

Turbidity and shading compress the photic layer, reduce chlorophyll maximum depth, and dampen diel swings in surface biomass; estuarine and river comparisons show an order-of-magnitude reduction in diel DO amplitude where production is limited. <cite id="c7a4684e-0">Where turbidity is high, diel DO cycling amplitudes can be an order of magnitude smaller due to limited production</cite>. Seasonal reservoir studies show significant diurnal fluctuations in temperature, oxygen, and CO2 that drive planktonic vertical movements and activity rhythms, implying robust diel community reorganization even in small, shallow systems. <cite id="c7a4684e-1">Diurnal fluctuations in multiple physico-chemical variables were significant in a reservoir and were linked to diurnal movement of plankters</cite>. Across riverine systems, phytoplankton often peak in rainy seasons due to dilution and nutrients, but diel-scale peaks within days around sunrise/sunset are consistent with light-driven physiology; zooplankton responses can vary with discharge-mediated habitat availability and predation risk. <cite id="47406f93-2">In a river impacted by effluent, phytoplankton abundance was higher in rainy months in the river but decreased with rain in a stream, with discharge releasing zooplankton from the benthos and littoral zone</cite> <cite id="47406f93-3">Daily-integrated production and biomass vary along river gradients, reflecting hydrology and nutrient availability</cite>.

# Methods and sampling design: capturing diel periodicity

Low-frequency sampling (e.g., only daytime vs nighttime snapshots) can miss the timing and magnitude of transitions; high-frequency designs (every 2–4 hours over 24 h) better resolve peaks, troughs, and behavioral switches. <cite id="47406f93-3">Species composition and activity patterns in lowland rivers of different sizes showed dusk peaks and diel declines in richness and abundance, highlighting the need for multiple daytime intervals</cite> <cite id="47406f93-0">Zooplankton collected over 24 h at 2–4 h intervals captured midday migration accentuation of export</cite> <cite id="c7a4684e-3">Many studies rely on only two to four hours sampled per day/night; high-frequency designs every three or two hours reveal precise timing of diel changes</cite>. For phytoplankton, diel oxygen curves and chlorophyll profiles integrate production and vertical transport; combining daytime epilimnetic maxima with nighttime loss via respiration/sinking provides quantitative amplitude estimates. <cite id="47406f93-3">Primary production in flowing waters is commonly evaluated from diurnal open-water oxygen curves and converted to daily integrals</cite> <cite id="75c05ea6-4">Daytime microstratification and nighttime cooling drive vertical redistribution of phytoplankton, visible as chlorophyll maxima migrations and 24-hour periodicity in fluorescence and backscatter</cite>.

# Cross-system context and river-specific nuances

Rivers span a spectrum from highly turbid, fast-flowing channels to clearer backwaters and floodplains. In turbid systems, the diel cycle is often dominated by strong daytime production followed by rapid nighttime losses; in clearer reaches, DVM and layered structures can create pronounced vertical and temporal partitioning. <cite id="c7a4684e-0">High turbidity reduces production and damps diel oxygen amplitude</cite> <cite id="75c05ea6-4">Daytime thermal microstratification drives sedimentation while nighttime cooling induces resuspension</cite>. River–lake interfaces and cascade systems show that hydrologic connectivity can synchronize or amplify diel cycles: lake zooplankton exported into streams at midday via DVM can reinforce downstream diel backscatter and nutrient pulses, while cascade reservoirs alter light, nutrients, and biotic interactions that shape longitudinal plankton patterns. <cite id="47406f93-0">Midday DVM accentuates zooplankton export from lakes to streams</cite> <cite id="47406f93-4">Hydrology, nutrients, and biotic interactions control phytoplankton and zooplankton composition and biomass, with predation interactions making single-species explanations incomplete</cite>.

# Synthesis: What to expect in rivers

- Expect strong diel periodicity: phytoplankton biomass and photosynthesis peak during daylight hours; at night, respiration and sinking reduce surface biomass unless compensated by night-time entrainment or upstream export. Zooplankton typically migrate upward at night to feed on daytime production and return during the day, producing clear diel backscatter and community oscillations. <cite id="75c05ea6-2">Diel light:dark cycles regulate phytoplankton metabolic processes</cite> <cite id="75c05ea6-3">Photosynthetic maxima peak at noon, with species-specific division timing</cite> <cite id="75c05ea6-4">24-hour periodicity in chlorophyll-related signals reflects nonphotochemical quenching and/or diurnal convective mixing</cite> <cite id="c7a4684e-2">Diel backscatter peaks indicate ongoing zooplankton DVM, persisting even under low overall abundance</cite>.

- Magnitude depends on context: daily integrated production in large rivers commonly ranges from tens to >100 mg C m−2 day−1 in slow-flowing reaches, with peaks during sunny periods and lower amplitudes under high turbidity; discharge events add thermal and optical pulses that can double or triple diel variability over hours. <cite id="47406f93-3">Congo: 64–434 mg C m−2 day−1 (falling water) and 52–248 mg C m−2 day−1 (high water); Danube reach peak 12.6 g O2 m−2 day−1</cite> <cite id="c7a4684e-0">Amplitudes can drop by an order of magnitude under high turbidity due to limited production</cite> <cite id="c7a4684e-2">A 13-hour flow peak followed by elevated backscatter over ~25 m depth illustrates discharge-driven diel-to-semidiel variability</cite>.

- Community reorganization is diel-scale: plankton assemblages often show dusk-to-night shifts in activity and composition, with peaks at twilight and declines through day or night depending on species traits and habitat availability. <cite id="47406f93-0">Species richness peaked at dusk and decreased through 24 h across lowland rivers</cite> <cite id="c7a4684e-1">Reservoir plankton assemblages tracked diurnal physico-chemical cycles, with significant diurnal fluctuations in temperature, oxygen, and CO2</cite>.

- Sampling must be high-frequency to capture timing and avoid biased inferences; integrate light, temperature, turbidity, and flow telemetry with 2–4 hour sampling over 24 h to quantify phase (dawn vs dusk peaks), amplitude, and hydrologic covariation. <cite id="c7a4684e-3">Low-frequency sampling reduces diel analyses to simple day/night comparisons; high-frequency designs at 2–3 hour intervals reveal precise timing</cite> <cite id="47406f93-0">24-hour 2–4 h sampling captured midday migration-driven export pulses</cite>.

# Open questions and practical guidance

Key uncertainties remain about the quantitative biomass swings of phytoplankton and zooplankton across small headwaters versus mainstem reaches, and how episodic hypoxia, contaminants, and macrophyte interactions modulate diel cycles. Comparative, high-frequency, light–temperature–turbidity–flow–resolved diel monitoring is needed to separate endogenous rhythms from hydrodynamic red noise. For applied work, plan 24-hour sampling at 2–4 h cadence, measure turbidity and irradiance, and align sampling with local sunrise/sunset; in turbid or highly dynamic reaches, expect smaller diel amplitudes and larger discharge-driven episodic peaks, requiring at least hourly adjustments during pulses. <cite id="c7a4684e-0">High turbidity reduces diel amplitude by limiting production</cite> <cite id="c7a4684e-2">Discharge pulses can impose strong diel-to-semidiel backscatter variability over a 12–24 hour window</cite> <cite id="c7a4684e-3">High-frequency sampling reveals timing of diel changes missed by day/night snapshots</cite>.

Snippet: Marine phytoplankton plays a pivotal role in Earth's ecosystems, acting as primary producers by contributing to ∼45% of global photosynthetic net primary production (Field et al. 1998). Consequently, it not only sustains the existence of most oceanic life but also supports life across the entire planet. Light availability has a profound impact on marine phytoplankton growth and physiology (Edwards et al. 2015). Earth's rotation produces the most pervasive rhythmic environmental signal, giving rise to alternating cycles of days (light periods or photoperiods) and nights (dark periods or skotoperiods), collectively known as diel cycles. Earth's tilted rotational axis and its translation around the Sun also lead to photoperiodic variations in diel cycles, resulting in long days (LDs) in summer and short days (SDs) in winter in temperate zones, the regions between the tropics and the polar circles. Seasonality plays a central regulatory role in marine phytoplankton dynamics (Bolaños et al. 2020;Chen et al. 2021;Mondal and Banerjee 2022). However, the different molecular rhythms underpinning these responses are not yet characterized. 

Chronobiology is a multidisciplinary field that focuses on the study of the timing and regulation of biological rhythms and their synchronization with environmental cycles (Kuhlman et al. 2018). Specifically, the autonomous oscillating molecular systems that have evolved to anticipate and respond to diel cycles are referred to as circadian clocks. These systems are entrained to external inputs, diel cycles, and produce rhythmic output of biological processes. Circadian rhythms are self-sustained, maintaining rhythmicity of about 24 h under constant conditions. To distinguish these biological rhythms from diel rhythms that respond to the environment, chronobiology experiments are typically designed as a sequence of several consecutive days under alternating light/dark cycles, followed by several consecutive days of constant light (LL) or dark (DD), called free-running conditions (Kuhlman et al. 2018).

Photoperiod varies seasonally at temperate to high latitudes, from total darkness during the high latitude winter, to constant illumination during the summer solstice. At mid-latitudes, photoperiod waxes and wanes through the year on top of shorter term changes in light intensity imposed by mixing. Photoperiod length interacts with light intensity (Brand and Guillard 1981) and with the oscillation pattern (Orefice et al. 2016) to modulate photosynthesis and metabolism in diatoms, whose photosynthesis involves tight coupling between chloroplasts and mitochondria (Prihoda et al. 2012, Bailleul et al. 2015). Yet, surprisingly few studies (Chisholm and Costello 1980, Brand and Guillard 1981, Tilzer and Dubinsky 1987, Nielsen 1997, Tang and Vincent 2000, Walter et al. 2015) have systematically examined the effects of photoperiod on marine phytoplankton metabolism and physiology. In contrast, a recent meta-analysis attempted to extrapolate phytoplankton growth responses to light intensity from data derived from studies with different applied photoperiods (Edwards et al. 2015). 

Growth, photosynthetic, and adaptive traits are strongly influenced by organism size (McMahon and Bonner 1983, Peters 1983, Kooijman 1986, West et al. 1997, Marañ on et al. 2007, 2013). Diatoms span a wide range of sizes (Beardall et al. 2009) and their metabolism and photophysiology show predictable patterns across related species of increasing size (Finkel 2001, Finkel et al. 2004, Key et al. 2010, Wu et al. 2014a,b). Specific factors known to cycle on a diel basis (i.e., diel periodicity) among phytoplankton include population density, biomass, community species composition, intracellular metabolism, resources (e.g., nutrients, organic constituents, DNA concentration), enzymatic activity, and primary production (Prezelin, 1992). Early fieldbased studies acknowledged these diel cycles, and began investigating the influence that timeof-collection for sampling might have on aquatic plankton research (Maxwell and Mikihiko, 1957;Yentsch and Ryther, 1957;Shimada, 1958;Doty, 1959). By the 1960s, green algae, dinoflagellates, and diatoms had all been observed to have diel patterns in vitro (Holmes and Haxo, 1958;Hastings et al., 1961). Generally, this diel cycle of phytoplankton has been thought to be decoupled from ambient light (Harding et al., 1981;Yoshikawa and Furuya, 2006). Still, higher resolution of this cycle in various algal systems during experimentation enhances the reproducibility of results. In a cell division periodicity study of 26 clonal cultures of marine algal cultures (representing 13 species), it was found that intraspecific variation does occur, and that different algal species can exhibit diel periodicity with division occurring at night or during the day (Nelson and Brand, 1979). For example, it was found that in phytoplankton collected from Sagami Bay (Japan), photosynthetic maxima (normalized absorption; mol C m −2 h −1 ) were highest at noon, and lower at dawn and dusk, with end-of-day timepoints being significantly variable (Yoshikawa and Furuya, 2006). Title: Trophic interactions across lake–stream boundaries in mountain lakes
Snippet: Based on the rapid reduction of zooplankton abundance with increasing distance from lakes as shown by previous studies (Chandler 1937, Chang et al. 2008, Doi et al. 2008), zooplankton samples in streams below lakes were collected at 1, 10, 50, 100, 200, and 500 m below the first riffle at approximately the same time as lacustrine samples. Diel variation in zooplankton export from lakes to streams was evaluated for Thunder Lake, with fish, and Bluebird Lake, with no fish. Zooplankton were collected 1 m downstream of the lake over 24 h at intervals of 2 to 4 h. Longitudinal sampling of the downstream waters was conducted at all distances mentioned earlier at midday vertical migration accentuates export of zooplankton from lakes to streams.

Title: Plankton Abundance and Physico-chemical Water Quality of Effluent Impacted Waterbodies in Ile-Ife, Nigeria
Snippet: Generally, from the two sites, Chaoborus sp., Trichocerca similis, Brachionus falcatus and Filinia pejleri were found to be abundant sequentially. 

In the stream, phytoplankton showed higher abundance during the rainy months of June to September, while they showed higher abundance during the dry months in the river (Table 2). However, abundance of phytoplankton decreases with rain in the stream with members of the families of Chrysophyceae, Dinophyceae, Xanthophyceae, Dictyophyceae being absent in the stream by December. A gradual raise in abundance was observed in the zooplankton population of the sampled river through the rainy months. The increase in zooplankton abundance with rain has been attributed to flood discharge resulting in release of many organisms out of the river bed or littoral zone (Adeniyi and Adedeji, 2007). Meanwhile, the recorded overall plankton abundant in the stream than Opa River such that 6 out of 8 recorded phytoplankton families, and 4 out of 5 zooplankton groups, as well as higher planktonic abundance in the stream could be linked to nutrient constituent of the stream (Table 2). 

Phytoplankton members of the Families Chlorophyceae, Cyanophyceae, Euglenophyceae were abundantly present in the months of July and August (Table 2). The highest abundance of plankton species was recorded in September and October. This could be attributed to the peak of rainfall and favourable physicochemical parameters due to dilution of water bodies which neutralised the toxic effect of the effluent. However, low percentage occurrence of zooplankton was recorded in dry season. This correlates with the findings of Onwudinjo and Egborge (1994), who observed that in dry season, when salinity is high, few species were distributed within the deeper water. Egborge (1981) reported that zooplankton abundance is maximum only in dry season. This negates the result of the hereby study, as more zooplankton species occurred in rainy season.

Title: Photosynthesis, carbon acquisition and primary productivity of phytoplankton: a review dedicated to Colin Reynolds
Snippet: Primary production in flowing waters is commonly evaluated as community production in streams from diurnal open water oxygen curves (Cox, 2003;Webster et al., 2005;Uehlinger, 2006). Estimates of plankton production in large rivers are not as common as assessments in lakes. Several ecologists have argued that the characteristics of many large rivers, deep and turbid, prevent phytoplankton to be of any significant importance. In contrast, Reynolds (1994a, b) investigated river plankton intensively both theoretical (1988, 1996b) and practical (Reynolds & Glaister, 1989, 1993). A few investigations shall illustrate the present status. Production in tropical 123 Hydrobiologia stream and rivers is summarized by Davies et al. (2008). 

Daily integrated production measured in the mainstem along a 1700-km stretch of the Congo River, DR Kongo, Africa varied between 64.3 and 434.1 mg C m -2 day -1 in falling water conditions and between 51.5 and 247.6 mg C m -2 day -1 when water was high (Descy et al., 2017). Phytoplankton biomass in the Congo River was likely restricted by hydrological factors. Results from this study indicate that phytoplankton growth in the main channel of the Congo River can occur due to hydrological processes maintaining phytoplankton biomass even during high water. This contrasts with other tropical river systems where connectivity with the floodplain, the presence of natural lakes and man-made reservoirs play a prominent role in the recruitment of phytoplankton to the main river. 

During a longitudinal survey of the River Danube from km 2510 downstream to the delta (Dokulil, 2014b) instantaneous FRRF signals were obtained and converted to daily integral oxygen production (Fig. 3). Column production remained below 1 g O 2 m -2 day -1 in the upper reach until river km 1500 and increased thereafter rapidly up to 12.6 g O 2 m -2 day -1 at river km 1262 (Fig. 3B).

Title: Hydrodynamics Regulate Longitudinal Plankton Community Structure in an Alpine Cascade Reservoir System
Snippet: Plankton, including phytoplankton and zooplankton, plays an important role in material circulation and energy flow in river or aquatic ecosystems (Cury et al., 2000;Richardson and Schoeman, 2004;Frederiksen et al., 2006). Phytoplankton is the main primary producer, whereas zooplankton is a group connecting the food webs of river ecosystems and are the most sensitive species to changes (Padisák et al., 2000;Silva et al., 2005;Perbiche-Neves and Nogueira, 2010;Wang et al., 2018). Therefore, community characteristics and dynamics of plankton are often used to explore the structure and functioning of river ecosystems, help in identifying regulating factors of plankton dynamics, and in evaluating effects of human activities on natural river ecosystems (Paerl et al., 2010;Okuku et al., 2016). 

Previous studies on phytoplankton or zooplankton in individual reservoir reported that hydrology, nutrient availability, and biota interactions were the main controlling factors of plankton composition and biomass in reservoirs (Rangel et al., 2012;Beaver et al., 2013;Chang et al., 2014;Silva et al., 2014;Amaral et al., 2020). However, the detailed relationship between plankton community and these environmental factors was reservoir specific and more complex since conflicting results were reported (Beaver et al., 2013;Silva et al., 2014). Previous studies on the plankton pattern formation mechanism in reservoirs that omitted either phytoplankton or zooplankton may be inaccurate owing to the predation relationship between phytoplankton and zooplankton (Chang et al., 2014). Lack of a detailed investigation on environmental variables, phytoplankton, zooplankton, and fish characteristics may partly account for the contradicting findings from previous studies (Chang et al., 2014). Although studies on phytoplankton or zooplankton community in individual reservoirs are abundant, studies on longitudinal plankton community pattern and corresponding structuring factors after cascade reservoir construction are few (Okuku et al., 2016).

Photoperiod length interacts with light intensity (Brand and Guillard 1981) and with the oscillation pattern (Orefice et al. 2016) to modulate photosynthesis and metabolism in diatoms, whose photosynthesis involves tight coupling between chloroplasts and mitochondria (Prihoda et al. 2012, Bailleul et al. 2015). Yet, surprisingly few studies (Chisholm and Costello 1980, Brand and Guillard 1981, Tilzer and Dubinsky 1987, Nielsen 1997, Tang and Vincent 2000, Walter et al. 2015) have systematically examined the effects of photoperiod on marine phytoplankton metabolism and physiology. In contrast, a recent meta-analysis attempted to extrapolate phytoplankton growth responses to light intensity from data derived from studies with different applied photoperiods (Edwards et al. 2015). 

Growth, photosynthetic, and adaptive traits are strongly influenced by organism size (McMahon and Bonner 1983, Peters 1983, Kooijman 1986, West et al. 1997, Marañ on et al. 2007, 2013). Diatoms span a wide range of sizes (Beardall et al. 2009) and their metabolism and photophysiology show predictable patterns across related species of increasing size (Finkel 2001, Finkel et al. 2004, Key et al. 2010, Wu et al. 2014a,b). At least two broad categories of mechanisms conceptually connect organism size, photoperiod, light intensity, and growth rate.

documents.snippet: Diel patterns in phytoplankton are common. Specific factors known to cycle on a diel basis (i.e., diel periodicity) among phytoplankton include population density, biomass, community species composition, intracellular metabolism, resources (e.g., nutrients, organic constituents, DNA concentration), enzymatic activity, and primary production (Prezelin, 1992). Early fieldbased studies acknowledged these diel cycles, and began investigating the influence that timeof-collection for sampling might have on aquatic plankton research (Maxwell and Mikihiko, 1957;Yentsch and Ryther, 1957;Shimada, 1958;Doty, 1959). By the 1960s, green algae, dinoflagellates, and diatoms had all been observed to have diel patterns in vitro (Holmes and Haxo, 1958;Hastings et al., 1961). Generally, this diel cycle of phytoplankton has been thought to be decoupled from ambient light (Harding et al., 1981;Yoshikawa and Furuya, 2006). Still, higher resolution of this cycle in various algal systems during experimentation enhances the reproducibility of results. In a cell division periodicity study of 26 clonal cultures of marine algal cultures (representing 13 species), it was found that intraspecific variation does occur, and that different algal species can exhibit diel periodicity with division occurring at night or during the day (Nelson and Brand, 1979). For example, it was found that in phytoplankton collected from Sagami Bay (Japan), photosynthetic maxima (normalized absorption; mol C m −2 h −1 ) were highest at noon, and lower at dawn and dusk, with end-of-day timepoints being significantly variable (Yoshikawa and Furuya, 2006). Thus, photosynthetic variations were thought to be endogenously regulated (Behrenfeld et al., 2004).

# Overview

Synchronized diurnal periodicity in river plankton arises from coupled physical–biological mechanisms that rhythmically restructure the water column and reshape planktonic access to light, nutrients, habitat, and predators. During the day, solar heating, flow regimes, and organismal behaviors conspire to concentrate primary producers near the surface; at night, cooling, reduced shear, and hydrodynamic mixing redistribute cells vertically and laterally, resetting spatial patterns and abundance peaks in a reproducible daily cycle. <cite id="36a3f358-0">Diel solar heating produces a stratified epilimnion with a thermocline that suppresses turbulent mixing in the daytime, while nocturnal cooling relaxes stratification and enhances mixing</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-1">These diel fluctuations in stratification are tightly linked to phytoplankton abundance and vertical differences in rivers</cite>. <cite id="a7213263-2">Zooplankton also show diurnal vertical redistribution in river channels, often with greater abundances deeper during the day due to daily vertical migrations that help avoid fish predators</cite>.

# Thermal–Hydrodynamic Forcing: Diel Stratification, Mixing, and Light Partitioning

Solar radiation imposes a 24‑hour thermal and dynamical rhythm by repeatedly charging and draining the river thermal stratification battery. <cite id="36a3f358-0">Daytime shortwave flux warms the surface, generating a non‑uniform stable thermocline that damps turbulent mixing; at night, the absence of radiation relaxes temperature gradients and increases turbulent mixing</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-0">The resulting diel modulation of mixing controls scalar and organism transport, with extreme stratification limiting oxygen and nutrient exchange and producing hypoxia in benthic regions; rapid destratification can overturn oxygenated surface waters with anoxic bottom waters, with ecosystem consequences</cite>. 

Thermal stratification directly partitions light among the plankton community by confining photosynthesis to the daytime euphotic surface layer. <cite id="36a3f358-2">Rivers are increasingly recognized as stratifying systems due to hydrologic alterations; river stratification controls mixing depth, light availability, and mixing interval, shaping phytoplankton distribution and community composition</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-1">Strong daytime stratification maintains cyanobacteria in surface waters, amplifying bloom intensity, whereas at night destratification can homogenize vertical distributions</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-3">In shallow rivers, the diel thermocline migrates vertically through the water column and can reach the riverbed at night, differentiating river stratification from lakes</cite>. 

The net effect is a synchronized daily rhythm of vertical concentration and dilution. <cite id="36a3f358-4">Modeling shows that turbulence and stratification jointly determine vertical mixing and light exposure; greater nighttime turbulence in a cool season brought more deeper phytoplankton into the euphotic zone, increasing 24‑hour integrated production</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-0">Reduced turbulence under persistent stratification (e.g., low flow drought conditions) concentrates biomass near the surface, as observed in outbreaks of cyanobacteria and algal blooms with associated oxygen depletion</cite>.

# Biological Responses: Phytoplankton Vertical Accumulation and Diel Migration

Phytoplankton respond to diel hydro-thermal forcing with synchronized abundance and vertical patterning. <cite id="36a3f358-1">Cyanobacteria often accumulate in the epilimnion during daytime stratification and maintain surface concentrations through buoyancy strategies that exploit diel fluctuations, leading to high chlorophyll a values in surface water that decline as the thermocline deepens</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-1">Motile taxa exhibit striking regular vertical migrations (e.g., across a 10 °C gradient) at night and back to surface early morning, whereas non‑motile phytoplankton maintain more constant vertical distributions</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-3">Such diel thermocline migration reshapes the vertical structure of phytoplankton populations across the entire water column</cite>. 

These behaviors are tightly coupled to river hydrodynamics and regulation. <cite id="36a3f358-2">River stratification is more prevalent in modified systems; in regulated rivers, stratification positively associates with phytoplankton abundance and vertical differences when cyanobacteria are abundant, consistent with stratification maintaining surface accumulation and amplifying blooms</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-0">Flow regulation and drought reduce turbulence production and strengthen stratification, producing long periods of surface biomass accumulation with downstream ecological impacts</cite>.

# Zooplankton Behavioral Synchrony: Vertical Migration, Predation Risk, and Tidal Forcing

Zooplankton synchronize vertical positions with the diel cycle to balance light for phytoplanktivores and predator avoidance, and with tidal/flow regimes in river–estuary transitions. <cite id="a7213263-2">In rivers, zooplankton abundance tends to be greater at greater depths during the day due to daily vertical migrations that avoid fish predators, demonstrating predator‑mediated diel synchronization</cite>. <cite id="a7213263-2">Conversely, shoreline macrophyte backwaters and boulders alter local hydraulics, with backwaters reducing velocity and creating retention that can enhance zooplankton richness and abundance, while high turbulence at river structures mixes water and can homogenize vertical distributions</cite>. 

Tidal and stormflow forcing imprint rhythms on zooplankton distributions in tidal reaches. <cite id="a7213263-1">River–estuarine copepods perform tidal vertical migration, shifting lower in the water column on ebb tides to maintain position against residual flows; heavy rainfall and dam releases can temporarily sweep zooplankton out of tidal reaches, yet populations rapidly return after flooding, indicating strong behavioral coupling to hydrodynamics</cite>. At broader scales, connectivity dynamics modulate abundance on diel to seasonal scales. <cite id="a7213263-3">Floodplain–channel coupling: temporary cessation of floodplain inflows into the main channel sharply drops river zooplankton abundance, while rises in water level trigger organism transport and can predict short‑term zooplankton highs/lows; thus, hydrograph dynamics set the stage for synchronized diurnal to diel‑seasonal rhythms</cite>. <cite id="a7213263-4">Seasonal water‑level fluctuations of several meters in large river–floodplain systems are hypothesized to drive sharp zooplankton fluctuations, highlighting the leading role of hydrologic forcing</cite>.

# River-Specific Hydrodynamics: Helical/Secondary Flows, Confluences, and Regulation

Meandering and compound channels generate secondary circulations that synchronize cross‑channel patchiness with the diel cycle by steering, retaining, and mixing water across depth and width. <cite id="a83d9dc3-1">In curved channels, centrifugal forcing and bed‑return flows create helical secondary currents: surface flow moves toward the outer bank and near‑bed flow toward the inner bank, producing vertical recirculation that redistributes suspended loads and organisms, shaping diel and tidal patchiness across bends</cite>. <cite id="a83d9dc3-3">These helical flows and recirculation zones produce complex secondary flows and recirculation cells that trap and advect tracers and particles, imprinting time‑varying concentration peaks and lulls across the channel</cite>. At confluences, density–stratified inflows interact to form helical and lock‑exchange structures that control mixing timing and spatial zonation. <cite id="a83d9dc3-2">Counter‑rotating helical cells at a large river–lake confluence direct mixing toward one bank while blocking counterflow, producing asymmetric diel mixing and vertical interfaces; daytime vs nighttime density contrasts modulate whether surface or bed flows dominate, reorganizing vertical distributions on diel timescales</cite>. 

Water management and flow regulation overwrite or entrain natural diel rhythms by altering near‑surface turbulence and diel velocity profiles. <cite id="a83d9dc3-4">In a regulated river, demand‑following hydropower produced diel changes from ~0.2–0.3 m s⁻¹ daytime flow to near‑zero at night, shifting hydrodynamics from lotic to lentic and modulating oxygen flux into sediments by a factor of two</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-2">Such regulation reduces diel turbulence-driven mixing, promotes persistent stratification, and concentrates phytoplankton and cyanobacteria in surface waters, aligning community distributions and abundance peaks with daytime light and flow minima</cite>. In tidal and ebb–flood regimes, vertical and horizontal distributions shift systematically with the tide. <cite id="a7213263-1">Copepods systematically lower their depth at night on ebb tides to counter residual outflows, and extreme surge events can transiently strip tidal reaches of zooplankton before rapid repopulation</cite>.

# Mechanisms Linking Hydrodynamics to Spatial Distribution Patterns

- Cross‑channel zonation by helical and bend‑driven recirculation: <cite id="a83d9dc3-1">Helical flows sweep near‑surface water toward the outer bank and return near‑bed flow to the inner bank, creating asymmetric vertical and lateral distributions of suspended cells and nutrients</cite>. <cite id="a83d9dc3-3">Recirculation zones in bends trap and slowly exchange water, producing elevated concentrations at both early and late times in tracer breakthrough curves, analogous to diel‑scales buildup and flushing</cite>. 
- Hydraulic retention and connectivity: <cite id="a7213263-2">Backwaters and vegetated microhabitat reduce velocity and enhance lateral retention, elevating zooplankton richness and abundance; conversely, high‑turbulence features homogenize distributions</cite>. <cite id="a7213263-3">At the river–floodplain scale, water‑level rises introduce enriched waters and organisms, while falls isolate the channel, producing sharp spatial and temporal shifts in abundance</cite>.
- Diel mixing depth and tide/flow modulation: <cite id="36a3f358-3">Diel thermocline migration can reach the riverbed in shallow systems, synchronizing vertical heterogeneity across depth</cite>. <cite id="a83d9dc3-4">Regulation narrows diel velocity ranges, homogenizing near‑surface dynamics and oxygen availability across the channel</cite>. <cite id="a7213263-1">In tidal reaches, ebb–flood cycles synchronize vertical migration with horizontal transport, producing coherent spatiotemporal patterns</cite>.

# Ecosystem Coupling: Light, Production, and Trophic Synchrony

Diel reorganization of vertical niches coordinates producer–consumer dynamics. <cite id="36a3f358-1">Daytime stratification concentrates cyanobacteria in the euphotic zone, enhancing growth and biomass</cite>, while nighttime mixing redistributes cells and nutrients. <cite id="36a3f358-4">Increased nighttime turbulence in spring brought deeper phytoplankton into light, increasing daily integrated production</cite>. Zooplanktivorous taxa align their activity with prey availability and risk structure. <cite id="a7213263-2">River zooplankton accumulate deeper during the day to avoid fish predators, demonstrating predator‑mediated vertical synchrony that can cascade into phytoplankton dynamics via grazing</cite>. In river–estuary junctions, hydrodynamic sorting and tidal migrations refine trophic patch networks that reset each cycle. <cite id="a83d9dc3-2">Helical and lock‑exchange flows at confluences produce asymmetric mixing interfaces that organize vertical zonation and lateral plumes</cite>. 

# Exceptions, Variability, and Controls Across River Types

Mechanisms scale with river order, morphology, and management. <cite id="36a3f358-2">Shallow, warm, and slow rivers and weir pools commonly show single thermoclines that migrate diel‑ly and maintain surface phytoplankton accumulation</cite>, whereas deep systems can develop multiple thermoclines with more complex diel behavior. <cite id="a83d9dc3-3">Braided and multi‑subchannel rivers host multiple helical cells and recirculation zones that fragment cross‑channel coherence</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-0">Low‑flow droughts amplify stratification and surface accumulation, increasing harmful algal risk</cite>, while high‑flow events homogenize distributions. <cite id="a7213263-1">Dam releases and storm surges can strip plankton from tidal reaches but are followed by rapid recolonization</cite>. Seasonality overlays diel rhythms via water‑level amplitude and stratification intensity. <cite id="a7213263-4">Large river–floodplain systems with multi‑meter seasonal amplitude exhibit sharp zooplankton fluctuations, with water‑level rise/fall setting the tempo for daily‑seasonal cycles</cite>.

# Synthesis: Why Diel Patterns Synchronize

- Day–night thermal–hydrodynamic cycle: <cite id="36a3f358-0">Surface warming and stratification at night reduce mixing and concentrate biomass near the surface, while nocturnal cooling and turbulence homogenize the water column</cite>. 
- Flow‑structure feedbacks: <cite id="a83d9dc3-1">Helical/secondary flows in bends and along bars synchronize lateral transport with vertical migration, creating coherent cross‑channel patchiness</cite>; <cite id="a83d9dc3-2">confluence density and helical cells impose asymmetric mixing and interface tilting</cite>. 
- Behavioral entrainment: <cite id="36a3f358-1">Phytoplankton diel vertical migration across thermoclines</cite> and <cite id="a7213263-2">zooplankton predator‑mediated vertical movements</cite> lock community distributions to light and risk rhythms. 
- Tidal and hydrologic forcing: <cite id="a7213263-1">Tidal vertical migration and rapid flood‑driven entrainment in tidal reaches</cite> and <cite id="a7213263-3">floodplain connectivity via water‑level rise/fall</cite> imprint synchronized spatiotemporal cycles from estuary to main channel. 
- Regulation and morphology: <cite id="a83d9dc3-4">Flow regulation narrows diel turbulence and oxygen exchange</cite>, while <cite id="a83d9dc3-1">meanders and secondary currents</cite> generate persistent cross‑channel heterogeneity that co‑varies with the day–night cycle.

# Remaining Uncertainties and Research Needs

Quantifying the phase relationships between phytoplankton peaks, zooplankton grazing, and fish predation across river orders, and isolating the relative contributions of wind vs current near‑surface turbulence at different scales, remain active questions. <cite id="a83d9dc3-4">Near‑surface dissipation is co‑controlled by wind and current, with regulation shifting dominance from wind‑dominated estuarine regimes toward current‑controlled lotic behavior</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-2">Field studies consistently link river stratification to vertical differences and abundance, but causal disentangling of light vs nutrient vs predation effects requires manipulative experiments and high‑frequency multi‑sensor profiling</cite>. Future work that jointly observes diel hydrodynamics (velocity, stratification, turbulence), vertical distributions, and grazing mortality will refine mechanistic models of synchronized diel periodicity across river ecosystems. <cite id="36a3f358-0">Understanding diel mixing regimes and their ecological consequences is central to predicting harmful algal events and oxygen depletion linked to stratification extremes</cite>.

Title: How can river-estuarine planktonic copepods survive river floods?
Snippet: Some planktonic animals inhabiting the tidal reaches of rivers exhibit adaptive behaviors to maintain their position in the river against the residual tidal flow, that is, long-term average flow. A well-documented behavior is 'tidal vertical migration' (Haertel & Osterberg 1967;Cronin & Forward 1979;Wooldridge & Erasmus 1980;Hough & Naylor 1991;Morgan et al. 1997;Kimmerer et al. 1998). Plankters maintain their position in the tidal reaches by shifting the population lower in the water column on the ebb tide than on the flood tide. When a river is swollen because of heavy rainfall, water flow is much faster than usual, however, indigenous river-estuarine zooplankton will be swept out to sea in spite of such maintenance mechanisms. Because there have been no reported instances of river floods causing local extinction of estuarine zooplankton, it seems that these organisms succeed in surviving such natural events. There have been no studies to understand how river-estuarine zooplankton manage to do this. Possible ways to withstand river floods are to return quickly into the tidal reaches without significant population losses, to recover the population loss through subsequent reproduction, or both. The present study provides some data to demonstrate the mechanism actually employed. 

On 6-7 July 2001, we conducted a 24-h plankton survey in the lower tidal reaches of the Chikugo River, Kyushu. The objective of the survey was to monitor the tide-related vertical migration of the dominant planktonic copepods. In the morning of 6 July, however, there was a heavy rain, which had begun the previous night. The water at the study site flowed seaward much faster than usual, especially for several hours from the late morning, because a dam 23 km up the river released water by fully opening its water gate at 09:10. We completed the survey despite the severe field conditions, but we failed to take adequate data for showing tidal vertical migration because we could collect only a small number of copepods in the tidal reaches during the period of river flooding. Nonetheless, we could observe that copepods that once swept out from the tidal reaches returned quickly after the episode of flooding. The present study describes the phenomenon and presents an answer to the question of how they do this.

Snippet: Fluid undergoing rotational motion can be defined as rotational turbulence, with examples such as typhoons, tornadoes, and cyclones (Hu et al., 2022). The distribution characteristics of rotational turbulence are generally represented using helicity. For instance, in tornado studies, storm-relative helicity or updraft helicity is often employed to predict the probability of tornado occurrence (Malloy & Tippett, 2024). In this study, the entrainment process of water intake at the pumping station exhibited characteristics of rotational turbulence, making helicity an appropriate tool for characterizing this process. Furthermore, our validation shows that helicity was well-suited for describing the entrainment region in river water intakes. The envelope of helicity at a certain threshold closely aligned with the trajectory range of entrained particles (Figure 7). The helicity threshold varies across different scales of rotational turbulence. For example, Ding et al. (1996) used monitoring data from 33 severe weather events to determine a storm-relative helicity threshold of ≥90 m/s 2 for predicting tornadoes. In this study, the helicity threshold range for entrainment of fish eggs and larvae during water intake was found to be between 0.004 and 0.047 m/s 2 . In practical applications, the appropriate helicity threshold should be determined comprehensively, considering factors such as the specific intake structure and the intake flow rate. 

Both the intake flow rate and river flow rate affected the depth and width of the entrainment area. As the intake flow rate increased, both the depth and width of the entrainment area expanded. However, the river flow rate only influenced the depth of the entrainment area (Figure 8). This study selected an appropriate absolute helicity threshold to define the threat region, indicating that fish eggs and larvae which entering this area were at risk of entrainment. This region was characterized by strong vortex intensity, dense vortex distribution, and significant disturbances, accompanied by notable turbulence and mixing (Holm & Kerr, 2007). Fish eggs and larvae entering threat region would have a higher probability of being entrained into the intake box, with their trajectories deviating under the influence of entrainment.

The instability of the river channel flow tends to develop a curved channel pattern, in which the flow is forced to follow the channel's curvature; the centrifugal force thus created pushes the flow toward the outer bank, and the associated superelevation of the water surface drives the flow near the bed back toward the inner bank. The balance of these two forces creates a vertical recirculation, known as the helical flow or secondary current, in a channel bend. The upper part of the helical flow (near the water surface) is toward the outer bank, and the lower part (near bed) of the flow is toward the inner bank. Sediment transport in a curved channel is strongly affected by such a helical flow system. Since more sediment particles are distributed near the bed in a vertical profile, the helical current distributes more sediment load to the inner bank and less sediment to the outer bank. As a result, erosion would occur along the outer bank and deposition along the inner bank. Inevitably, a skewed channel cross section is developed in channel bends with a lower bed near the outer bank and higher bed near the inner bank. In turn, more and more flow would be distributed along the outer bank, causing erosion and mechanic instability of the outer bank. The fundamental theory of the curved channel fluid dynamics has been established by Rozovskii [31]. Snippet: Rivers are dynamic systems of nature that have meandering curves and sinuous channel patterns. These meandering shapes of rivers significantly influence the topography and flow dynamics of water flow. Meandering rivers are characterized by continuous lateral shifts in their channels, giving rise to patterns that influence the velocity and behavior of water flow within them [1]. This induces complex flow characteristics including secondary flows and recirculation zones, which have significant effects on the transport of contaminants within rivers. In meandering rivers, the flow velocity creates recirculation, which forms complex patterns of water movement and secondary flows [2]. One notable feature associated with meandering river channels is the development of helical secondary flows [3][4][5]. These helical flows, which resemble corkscrew patterns, contribute to mixing within the river. Understanding the role of these flow characteristics is essential for comprehending the complex transport processes occurring in meandering rivers [6]. 

Furthermore, riverine dynamics are further complicated by the existence of flow recirculation zones in meandering rivers. Tracers and other materials carried by the flowing water are captured in these recirculation zones [7]. As a result, the movement of these tracers in the river becomes complex, and there is a chance that tracer concentration will be abnormally high at both the early and late stages of breakthrough curves due to captured tracers. Investigating these breakthrough curves can provide insights into the temporal evolution of tracer concentrations [8,9], which may offer valuable information about the transport mechanisms influenced by meander-driven flows.

# Overview

Synchronized diurnal periodicity in river plankton arises from coupled physical–biological mechanisms that rhythmically restructure the water column and reshape planktonic access to light, nutrients, habitat, and predators. During the day, solar heating, flow regimes, and organismal behaviors conspire to concentrate primary producers near the surface; at night, cooling, reduced shear, and hydrodynamic mixing redistribute cells vertically and laterally, resetting spatial patterns and abundance peaks in a reproducible daily cycle. <cite id="36a3f358-0">Diel solar heating produces a stratified epilimnion with a thermocline that suppresses turbulent mixing in the daytime, while nocturnal cooling relaxes stratification and enhances mixing</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-1">These diel fluctuations in stratification are tightly linked to phytoplankton abundance and vertical differences in rivers</cite>. <cite id="a7213263-2">Zooplankton also show diurnal vertical redistribution in river channels, often with greater abundances deeper during the day due to daily vertical migrations that help avoid fish predators</cite>.

# Thermal–Hydrodynamic Forcing: Diel Stratification, Mixing, and Light Partitioning

Solar radiation imposes a 24‑hour thermal and dynamical rhythm by repeatedly charging and draining the river thermal stratification battery. <cite id="36a3f358-0">Daytime shortwave flux warms the surface, generating a non‑uniform stable thermocline that damps turbulent mixing; at night, the absence of radiation relaxes temperature gradients and increases turbulent mixing</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-0">The resulting diel modulation of mixing controls scalar and organism transport, with extreme stratification limiting oxygen and nutrient exchange and producing hypoxia in benthic regions; rapid destratification can overturn oxygenated surface waters with anoxic bottom waters, with ecosystem consequences</cite>. 

Thermal stratification directly partitions light among the plankton community by confining photosynthesis to the daytime euphotic surface layer. <cite id="36a3f358-2">Rivers are increasingly recognized as stratifying systems due to hydrologic alterations; river stratification controls mixing depth, light availability, and mixing interval, shaping phytoplankton distribution and community composition</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-1">Strong daytime stratification maintains cyanobacteria in surface waters, amplifying bloom intensity, whereas at night destratification can homogenize vertical distributions</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-3">In shallow rivers, the diel thermocline migrates vertically through the water column and can reach the riverbed at night, differentiating river stratification from lakes</cite>. 

The net effect is a synchronized daily rhythm of vertical concentration and dilution. <cite id="36a3f358-4">Modeling shows that turbulence and stratification jointly determine vertical mixing and light exposure; greater nighttime turbulence in a cool season brought more deeper phytoplankton into the euphotic zone, increasing 24‑hour integrated production</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-0">Reduced turbulence under persistent stratification (e.g., low flow drought conditions) concentrates biomass near the surface, as observed in outbreaks of cyanobacteria and algal blooms with associated oxygen depletion</cite>.

# Biological Responses: Phytoplankton Vertical Accumulation and Diel Migration

Phytoplankton respond to diel hydro-thermal forcing with synchronized abundance and vertical patterning. <cite id="36a3f358-1">Cyanobacteria often accumulate in the epilimnion during daytime stratification and maintain surface concentrations through buoyancy strategies that exploit diel fluctuations, leading to high chlorophyll a values in surface water that decline as the thermocline deepens</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-1">Motile taxa exhibit striking regular vertical migrations (e.g., across a 10 °C gradient) at night and back to surface early morning, whereas non‑motile phytoplankton maintain more constant vertical distributions</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-3">Such diel thermocline migration reshapes the vertical structure of phytoplankton populations across the entire water column</cite>. 

These behaviors are tightly coupled to river hydrodynamics and regulation. <cite id="36a3f358-2">River stratification is more prevalent in modified systems; in regulated rivers, stratification positively associates with phytoplankton abundance and vertical differences when cyanobacteria are abundant, consistent with stratification maintaining surface accumulation and amplifying blooms</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-0">Flow regulation and drought reduce turbulence production and strengthen stratification, producing long periods of surface biomass accumulation with downstream ecological impacts</cite>.

# Zooplankton Behavioral Synchrony: Vertical Migration, Predation Risk, and Tidal Forcing

Zooplankton synchronize vertical positions with the diel cycle to balance light for phytoplanktivores and predator avoidance, and with tidal/flow regimes in river–estuary transitions. <cite id="a7213263-2">In rivers, zooplankton abundance tends to be greater at greater depths during the day due to daily vertical migrations that avoid fish predators, demonstrating predator‑mediated diel synchronization</cite>. <cite id="a7213263-2">Conversely, shoreline macrophyte backwaters and boulders alter local hydraulics, with backwaters reducing velocity and creating retention that can enhance zooplankton richness and abundance, while high turbulence at river structures mixes water and can homogenize vertical distributions</cite>. 

Tidal and stormflow forcing imprint rhythms on zooplankton distributions in tidal reaches. <cite id="a7213263-1">River–estuarine copepods perform tidal vertical migration, shifting lower in the water column on ebb tides to maintain position against residual flows; heavy rainfall and dam releases can temporarily sweep zooplankton out of tidal reaches, yet populations rapidly return after flooding, indicating strong behavioral coupling to hydrodynamics</cite>. At broader scales, connectivity dynamics modulate abundance on diel to seasonal scales. <cite id="a7213263-3">Floodplain–channel coupling: temporary cessation of floodplain inflows into the main channel sharply drops river zooplankton abundance, while rises in water level trigger organism transport and can predict short‑term zooplankton highs/lows; thus, hydrograph dynamics set the stage for synchronized diurnal to diel‑seasonal rhythms</cite>. <cite id="a7213263-4">Seasonal water‑level fluctuations of several meters in large river–floodplain systems are hypothesized to drive sharp zooplankton fluctuations, highlighting the leading role of hydrologic forcing</cite>.

Meandering and compound channels generate secondary circulations that synchronize cross‑channel patchiness with the diel cycle by steering, retaining, and mixing water across depth and width. <cite id="a83d9dc3-1">In curved channels, centrifugal forcing and bed‑return flows create helical secondary currents: surface flow moves toward the outer bank and near‑bed flow toward the inner bank, producing vertical recirculation that redistributes suspended loads and organisms, shaping diel and tidal patchiness across bends</cite>. <cite id="a83d9dc3-3">These helical flows and recirculation zones produce complex secondary flows and recirculation cells that trap and advect tracers and particles, imprinting time‑varying concentration peaks and lulls across the channel</cite>. - Cross‑channel zonation by helical and bend‑driven recirculation: <cite id="a83d9dc3-1">Helical flows sweep near‑surface water toward the outer bank and return near‑bed flow to the inner bank, creating asymmetric vertical and lateral distributions of suspended cells and nutrients</cite>. <cite id="a83d9dc3-3">Recirculation zones in bends trap and slowly exchange water, producing elevated concentrations at both early and late times in tracer breakthrough curves, analogous to diel‑scales buildup and flushing</cite>. 
- Hydraulic retention and connectivity: <cite id="a7213263-2">Backwaters and vegetated microhabitat reduce velocity and enhance lateral retention, elevating zooplankton richness and abundance; conversely, high‑turbulence features homogenize distributions</cite>. <cite id="a7213263-3">At the river–floodplain scale, water‑level rises introduce enriched waters and organisms, while falls isolate the channel, producing sharp spatial and temporal shifts in abundance</cite>.
- Diel mixing depth and tide/flow modulation: <cite id="36a3f358-3">Diel thermocline migration can reach the riverbed in shallow systems, synchronizing vertical heterogeneity across depth</cite>. <cite id="a83d9dc3-4">Regulation narrows diel velocity ranges, homogenizing near‑surface dynamics and oxygen availability across the channel</cite>. <cite id="a7213263-1">In tidal reaches, ebb–flood cycles synchronize vertical migration with horizontal transport, producing coherent spatiotemporal patterns</cite>.

# Ecosystem Coupling: Light, Production, and Trophic Synchrony

Diel reorganization of vertical niches coordinates producer–consumer dynamics. <cite id="36a3f358-1">Daytime stratification concentrates cyanobacteria in the euphotic zone, enhancing growth and biomass</cite>, while nighttime mixing redistributes cells and nutrients. <cite id="36a3f358-4">Increased nighttime turbulence in spring brought deeper phytoplankton into light, increasing daily integrated production</cite>. # Exceptions, Variability, and Controls Across River Types

Mechanisms scale with river order, morphology, and management. <cite id="36a3f358-2">Shallow, warm, and slow rivers and weir pools commonly show single thermoclines that migrate diel‑ly and maintain surface phytoplankton accumulation</cite>, whereas deep systems can develop multiple thermoclines with more complex diel behavior. <cite id="a83d9dc3-3">Braided and multi‑subchannel rivers host multiple helical cells and recirculation zones that fragment cross‑channel coherence</cite>. <cite id="36a3f358-0">Low‑flow droughts amplify stratification and surface accumulation, increasing harmful algal risk</cite>, while high‑flow events homogenize distributions. <cite id="a7213263-1">Dam releases and storm surges can strip plankton from tidal reaches but are followed by rapid recolonization</cite>. Seasonality overlays diel rhythms via water‑level amplitude and stratification intensity. <cite id="a7213263-4">Large river–floodplain systems with multi‑meter seasonal amplitude exhibit sharp zooplankton fluctuations, with water‑level rise/fall setting the tempo for daily‑seasonal cycles</cite>.

# Synthesis: Why Diel Patterns Synchronize

- Day–night thermal–hydrodynamic cycle: <cite id="36a3f358-0">Surface warming and stratification at night reduce mixing and concentrate biomass near the surface, while nocturnal cooling and turbulence homogenize the water column</cite>. 
- Flow‑structure feedbacks: <cite id="a83d9dc3-1">Helical/secondary flows in bends and along bars synchronize lateral transport with vertical migration, creating coherent cross‑channel patchiness</cite>; <cite id="a83d9dc3-2">confluence density and helical cells impose asymmetric mixing and interface tilting</cite>. 
- Behavioral entrainment: <cite id="36a3f358-1">Phytoplankton diel vertical migration across thermoclines</cite> and <cite id="a7213263-2">zooplankton predator‑mediated vertical movements</cite> lock community distributions to light and risk rhythms. 
- Tidal and hydrologic forcing: <cite id="a7213263-1">Tidal vertical migration and rapid flood‑driven entrainment in tidal reaches</cite> and <cite id="a7213263-3">floodplain connectivity via water‑level rise/fall</cite> imprint synchronized spatiotemporal cycles from estuary to main channel.

# Remaining Uncertainties and Research Needs

Title: Stratification and temporal evolution of mixing regimes in diurnally heated river flows
Snippet: Water bodies such as rivers, estuaries and canals are subject to diurnal solar radiation. This unsteady heating causes these channels to experience time-varying flow states within their diel cycle. During the day, the short-wave radiation at the free surface is transmitted and progressively absorbed through the water column, leading to a non-uniform stable thermocline. Therefore, stable stratification is stronger near the free surface and gradually weakens towards the channel bed. This stratification then acts to dampen the turbulent mixing within these regions. Accounting for the diurnal variation of solar fluxes, solar radiation tends to strengthen stratification while the absence of radiation will cause the temperature field to relax, increasing turbulent mixing [1]. This mixing determines the overall ecological health of the limnological ecosystems [2]. As turbulence becomes suppressed as a result of stratification due to daytime heating, in extreme cases, this reduction in mixing limits the transportation of scalars such as dissolved oxygen, sediments and nutrients, causing the benthic region of the water column to experience conditions of eutrophication or hypoxia [3][4][5]. 

Among Australian inland rivers, during long periods of drought and high radiative forcings, flow rates are significantly reduced, causing a decrease in the turbulence production from the shear at the bottom of the channel. These low flows and persistently stratified flow states contribute to the extensive algal outbreaks resulting in mass fish mortality as seen in the Menindee Region of NSW over the summer of 2018 and 2019 [6]. Cyanobacterial blooms contribute to oxygen depletion at the near-wall or bottom region of the river channel as their substantial biological matter sinks to the bottom of the channel and consumes the oxygen reserves for decomposition. If a rapid breakdown of stratification occurs, the sudden overturning of the oxygenated epilimnion layer with the anoxic hypolimnion layer will cause the water column to dilute and therefore suffocate the wildlife that concentrates in the previously oxygen-rich region [7]. Understanding the processes that affect the mixing and turbulence of diurnally heated stratified flows can help predict and mitigate these detrimental events.

Title: How can river-estuarine planktonic copepods survive river floods?
Snippet: Some planktonic animals inhabiting the tidal reaches of rivers exhibit adaptive behaviors to maintain their position in the river against the residual tidal flow, that is, long-term average flow. A well-documented behavior is 'tidal vertical migration' (Haertel & Osterberg 1967;Cronin & Forward 1979;Wooldridge & Erasmus 1980;Hough & Naylor 1991;Morgan et al. 1997;Kimmerer et al. 1998). Plankters maintain their position in the tidal reaches by shifting the population lower in the water column on the ebb tide than on the flood tide. When a river is swollen because of heavy rainfall, water flow is much faster than usual, however, indigenous river-estuarine zooplankton will be swept out to sea in spite of such maintenance mechanisms. Because there have been no reported instances of river floods causing local extinction of estuarine zooplankton, it seems that these organisms succeed in surviving such natural events. There have been no studies to understand how river-estuarine zooplankton manage to do this. Possible ways to withstand river floods are to return quickly into the tidal reaches without significant population losses, to recover the population loss through subsequent reproduction, or both. The present study provides some data to demonstrate the mechanism actually employed. 

On 6-7 July 2001, we conducted a 24-h plankton survey in the lower tidal reaches of the Chikugo River, Kyushu. The objective of the survey was to monitor the tide-related vertical migration of the dominant planktonic copepods. In the morning of 6 July, however, there was a heavy rain, which had begun the previous night. The water at the study site flowed seaward much faster than usual, especially for several hours from the late morning, because a dam 23 km up the river released water by fully opening its water gate at 09:10. We completed the survey despite the severe field conditions, but we failed to take adequate data for showing tidal vertical migration because we could collect only a small number of copepods in the tidal reaches during the period of river flooding. Nonetheless, we could observe that copepods that once swept out from the tidal reaches returned quickly after the episode of flooding. The present study describes the phenomenon and presents an answer to the question of how they do this.

Title: Zooplankton as an indicator of hydrological connectivity of the main channel and the floodplain in a large river system

Therefore, to maintain high plankton density in the river, its arrival from the floodplain should be uninterrupted. We consider water level fall as the second important condition for the beginning of the transport of organisms and its duration. In this regard, when estimating zooplankton density in large unregulated rivers with the developed floodplains, one should take account of the direction (fall or rise) of the river hydrograph. Moreover, water-level dynamics can become the basis for predicting zooplankton abundance in the unregulated rivers and assessing changes in fish feeding conditions during the growing season.

Title: Zooplankton as an indicator of hydrological connectivity of the main channel and the floodplain in a large river system
Snippet: It is common knowledge that a floodplain serves as a plankton supplier for a river channel (Amoros & Bornette, 2002;Wahl et al., 2008;Lansac-Tôha et al., 2009;Bozelli et al. 2015;Branco et al., 2018); however, the mechanisms of interaction between them are not fully understood. Title: Estimated Hydraulic Characteristics and the Entrainment of Fish Eggs and Larvae at a Pumped River‐Water Intake
Snippet: Fluid undergoing rotational motion can be defined as rotational turbulence, with examples such as typhoons, tornadoes, and cyclones (Hu et al., 2022). The distribution characteristics of rotational turbulence are generally represented using helicity. For instance, in tornado studies, storm-relative helicity or updraft helicity is often employed to predict the probability of tornado occurrence (Malloy & Tippett, 2024). In this study, the entrainment process of water intake at the pumping station exhibited characteristics of rotational turbulence, making helicity an appropriate tool for characterizing this process. Furthermore, our validation shows that helicity was well-suited for describing the entrainment region in river water intakes. The envelope of helicity at a certain threshold closely aligned with the trajectory range of entrained particles (Figure 7). The helicity threshold varies across different scales of rotational turbulence. For example, Ding et al. (1996) used monitoring data from 33 severe weather events to determine a storm-relative helicity threshold of ≥90 m/s 2 for predicting tornadoes. In this study, the helicity threshold range for entrainment of fish eggs and larvae during water intake was found to be between 0.004 and 0.047 m/s 2 . In practical applications, the appropriate helicity threshold should be determined comprehensively, considering factors such as the specific intake structure and the intake flow rate. 

Both the intake flow rate and river flow rate affected the depth and width of the entrainment area. As the intake flow rate increased, both the depth and width of the entrainment area expanded. However, the river flow rate only influenced the depth of the entrainment area (Figure 8). This study selected an appropriate absolute helicity threshold to define the threat region, indicating that fish eggs and larvae which entering this area were at risk of entrainment. This region was characterized by strong vortex intensity, dense vortex distribution, and significant disturbances, accompanied by notable turbulence and mixing (Holm & Kerr, 2007). Fish eggs and larvae entering threat region would have a higher probability of being entrained into the intake box, with their trajectories deviating under the influence of entrainment.

Title: Modeling River Morphodynamic Process Using a Depth-Averaged Computational Model and an Application to a Mountain River
Snippet: Alluvial rivers often have lateral movements: meandering or channel migration. The instability of the river channel flow tends to develop a curved channel pattern, in which the flow is forced to follow the channel's curvature; the centrifugal force thus created pushes the flow toward the outer bank, and the associated superelevation of the water surface drives the flow near the bed back toward the inner bank. Fluid undergoing rotational motion can be defined as rotational turbulence, with examples such as typhoons, tornadoes, and cyclones (Hu et al., 2022). The distribution characteristics of rotational turbulence are generally represented using helicity. For instance, in tornado studies, storm-relative helicity or updraft helicity is often employed to predict the probability of tornado occurrence (Malloy & Tippett, 2024). In this study, the entrainment process of water intake at the pumping station exhibited characteristics of rotational turbulence, making helicity an appropriate tool for characterizing this process. Furthermore, our validation shows that helicity was well-suited for describing the entrainment region in river water intakes. The envelope of helicity at a certain threshold closely aligned with the trajectory range of entrained particles (Figure 7). The helicity threshold varies across different scales of rotational turbulence. For example, Ding et al. (1996) used monitoring data from 33 severe weather events to determine a storm-relative helicity threshold of ≥90 m/s 2 for predicting tornadoes. In this study, the helicity threshold range for entrainment of fish eggs and larvae during water intake was found to be between 0.004 and 0.047 m/s 2 . In practical applications, the appropriate helicity threshold should be determined comprehensively, considering factors such as the specific intake structure and the intake flow rate. 

Both the intake flow rate and river flow rate affected the depth and width of the entrainment area. As the intake flow rate increased, both the depth and width of the entrainment area expanded. However, the river flow rate only influenced the depth of the entrainment area (Figure 8). This study selected an appropriate absolute helicity threshold to define the threat region, indicating that fish eggs and larvae which entering this area were at risk of entrainment. This region was characterized by strong vortex intensity, dense vortex distribution, and significant disturbances, accompanied by notable turbulence and mixing (Holm & Kerr, 2007). Fish eggs and larvae entering threat region would have a higher probability of being entrained into the intake box, with their trajectories deviating under the influence of entrainment.
